paper_title: Reading the Unreadable: Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution Needs Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) aims to recover high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs while preserving textual content. Existing methods treat this as a visual restoration problem, yet severely degraded text often cannot be read from local visual evidence alone. Humans instead read it by reasoning over image context, logical patterns, and prior knowledge. This raises a fundamental question: Does TAISR need reasoning? To answer this, we introduce two diagnostic tools. The first, ReasonText, is a human-curated benchmark that separates reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text. The second, Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), is a recognition-based metric that measures text restoration quality without text detection errors. Evaluating twelve recent super-resolution (SR) models, we find a consistent and substantial performance drop on reasoning-required text, revealing a systematic blind spot. Two observations point to a remedy. One is that text-conditioned SR models restore text substantially better when given ground-truth text. The other is that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can read degraded text in low-resolution images through reasoning. We therefore propose Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC), a training-free plug-in that uses an external MLLM to infer the degraded text and feeds the resulting caption to a text-conditioned SR model. RTC consistently improves all six text-conditioned SR models we evaluate, especially on reasoning-required text. Surprisingly, a real-world SR model with RTC can even outperform the TAISR model with RTC, suggesting that reasoning should be a core design axis for future TAISR.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Real-world image super-resolution (real-world SR) [16, 33] aims to recover high-resolution (HR) images from low-resolution (LR) inputs corrupted by unknown degradations. Recent advances [5, 9, 17, 31, 35, 38, 41] leverage text-to-image generation models [10, 18, 24, 26] as generative backbones, producing visually plausible details even from severely degraded inputs. However, such generative priors often fail to preserve the structural information present in the LR image [5, 9]. This issue is particularly severe for text, where altering single stroke can change its meaning entirely. To address this challenge, line of work has introduced text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) [13, 15, 23, 40], which restores full scene images while preserving textual content. Unlike scene text image super-resolution (STISR) [4, 32], which operates on cropped text patches, TAISR inherits the open-scene setting of real-world SR and targets text fidelity within full images. Existing TAISR methods augment the SR model with text-aware modules such as text detection [40], segmentation [13], or spotting [15, 23]. Although these modules improve the localization and restoration of textual regions, they remain centered on local visual evidence. By contrast, humans read what appears unreadable. When distant sign is nearly illegible, we can often still read it by reasoning from the surrounding context, logical patterns, or prior knowledge of brands, places, and vocabulary. Current TAISR pipelines lack explicit mechanisms for such reasoning and hallucinate characters where local evidence is insufficient (Figure 1). This gap raises the central question of this paper: Does TAISR need reasoning? Answering it requires measurement, yet current tools fall short in two ways. Existing benchmarks [23] do not distinguish reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text, and their evaluation protocols rely on text spotting models [20, 46], whose detection errors contaminate the measurement of text restoration quality. We address both shortcomings with two diagnostic tools. First, we introduce ReasonText, humancurated benchmark that assigns each text instance perception-grounded difficulty level, separating reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text. Second, we propose Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), text restoration metric that runs text recognition directly on ground-truth text regions of SR outputs, bypassing the text detection stage. Using these tools, we evaluate twelve recent real-world SR and TAISR models and find that every models accuracy drops sharply on reasoning-required text: the lowest GTTCA on locally recoverable text across all models (45.7%) still exceeds the highest on reasoning-required text (24.5%). This failure occurs regardless of architecture, generative backbone, or training paradigm, and persists even in models explicitly designed for text. These results answer our question: TAISR does need reasoning. What remains is how to supply it, and we start from two observations. First, text-conditioned SR models [5, 9, 15, 23, 37, 41] restore reasoning-required text substantially better when the ground-truth transcripts are provided in their captions. Second, modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) [12, 29] can infer locally unreadable text in LR images through reasoning. Building on these observations, we propose Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC). In RTC, an external MLLM infers the degraded text and writes it into caption, which then replaces the default caption of text-conditioned SR model. Since both models remain frozen, RTC is training-free and can be attached to any such model. Empirically, RTC consistently improves both real-world SR and TAISR models on ReasonText, and these gains carry over to the existing TAISR benchmarks [23], SA-Text-test and RealText. Surprisingly, the strongest real-world SR model [9] with RTC outperforms the strongest TAISR model [15] with RTC, even though the latter builds on the same backbone [10] and adds text-aware modules. This result suggests that, once reasoning is supplied, current text-aware modules may bring no additional benefit. Reasoning should therefore be core design axis for TAISR, and natural next step is to build it into the text-aware modules themselves. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce ReasonText, the first TAISR benchmark for evaluating reasoning-required text, and GTTCA, metric that measures text restoration quality free of text detection errors. We evaluate twelve recent real-world SR and TAISR models on ReasonText and show that every models accuracy drops sharply on reasoning-required text. We propose RTC, training-free plug-in that injects an external MLLMs reasoning into textconditioned SR models through captions. Extensive experiments show that RTC consistently improves both real-world SR and TAISR models.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Real-World Image Super-Resolution (Real-World SR). Real-world SR aims to recover HR images from LR inputs corrupted by diverse, unknown degradations. Early GAN-based methods [16, 33] improve perceptual quality with adversarial training [11], but often introduce visual artifacts. To avoid such artifacts and restore realistic details even under severe degradations, recent work instead builds on generative models with strong priors, including diffusion and autoregressive (AR) models. Multi-step diffusion-based methods [5, 9, 17, 31, 38, 41] adapt pretrained text-to-image diffusion models [10, 24, 26] to real-world SR with conditioning modules such as ControlNet-style adapters [44]. Few-step diffusion-based methods [34, 37, 43] reduce the inference cost of iterative denoising by starting the diffusion process from the LR image instead of Gaussian noise, or by distilling multi-step model into single step. AR-based methods [25, 35] adapt multimodal AR model [18] with post-training techniques from large language models. However, such strong priors can also hallucinate plausible yet incorrect details. This failure mode is especially problematic for text, where even minor deviation can alter the meaning. Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution (TAISR). Motivated by this failure mode, TAISR aims to restore full scene images while explicitly preserving textual content. TextSR [40] first detects text regions with an OCR model, then restores the text with its own STISR model and the rest of the image with real-world SR model [33]. TADiSR [13] adds text segmentation decoder to predict text masks jointly with the restored image. TeReDiff [23] and UniT [15] use text spotting module that takes diffusion features as input and predicts text to guide restoration. Despite these diverse designs, all of them remain centered on local visual evidence and do not consider the reasoning that humans use to read locally unreadable text. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Recent MLLMs [1, 12, 28, 29] have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities on benchmarks requiring joint visual and textual understanding [21, 42]. In image super-resolution, however, MLLMs have been used in much more limited way. Real-world SR methods [5, 9, 41] employ LLaVA-1.5 [19] to caption LR images, and UniT adopts Qwen2.5VL [2] to initialize text predictions. In both cases, the MLLM is an earlier-generation model with limited reasoning ability and serves only as perceptual front-end. In contrast, we leverage the reasoning capability of recent MLLMs to infer locally unreadable text.

sections.title: 3 TAISR Needs Reasoning
sections.content: In this section, we examine whether existing real-world SR and TAISR models can restore text that requires reasoning. In Section 3.1, we introduce ReasonText, benchmark that separates reasoningrequired text from locally recoverable text. In Section 3.2, we propose Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), metric that measures text restoration quality by recognizing text directly at ground-truth locations. Using these two tools, we evaluate twelve recent SR models in Section 3.3 and find that all of them suffer substantial accuracy drop on reasoning-required text. 3.1 ReasonText Benchmark Limitations of existing benchmarks. To evaluate whether SR models can restore reasoningrequired text, we need reasoning-required label for each LR text instance, but no existing benchmark provides one. SA-Text-test [23] might seem to meet this need at first glance, since it provides three LR versions of each HR image at different synthetic degradation strengths. However, degradation strength is an image-level attribute, so it does not indicate whether an individual text instance requires reasoning (Figure 2(a)). natural alternative is to add such labels to the existing benchmarks [23], SA-Text-test and RealText, but two of their characteristics rule this out. First, their text polygons and transcripts contain non-trivial errors, as they are produced by fully automatic pipelines without human verification (Figure 2(c)). Second, their images are cropped without considering the context of each text instance, leaving few instances that can be read through reasoning (Figure 2(d)). We therefore construct ReasonText with three key properties: (1) all text polygons and transcripts are annotated by humans, (2) each image is cropped to preserve the context of its text instances, and (3) each instance is labeled with perception-grounded difficulty level: readable from the text region alone, readable only with reasoning, or unreadable (Figure 2(b)). 3 Figure 2: ReasonText addresses gaps in existing TAISR benchmarks. (a) SA-Text-test assigns difficulty at the image level via three degradation strengths, which does not indicate whether each instance requires reasoning. (b) ReasonText instead labels each instance with perception-grounded difficulty level, separating reasoning-required from locally recoverable text. (c) ReasonText is constructed from human annotations, which remain reliable across diverse scenes. (d) ReasonText crops the image to preserve context needed to read reasoning-required text. Data collection and annotation. We build ReasonText on two real-world SR benchmarks, RealSRv3 [3] and DRealSR [36], which provide camera-captured LRHR pairs rather than synthetically degraded ones. Trained annotators first label word-level polygons, transcripts, and orientations for every alphanumeric text instance in each full HR image, and the labels go through multiple rounds of verification. They then crop square HR patch around each text instance, including any content related to that instance. Following the standard 4 SR setting [15, 23], we resize each HR patch to 512512 and its aligned LR patch to 128128. Difficulty labeling. We obtain the perception-grounded difficulty level of each text instance through two-stage labeling process. Both stages follow the same protocol. Five of ten annotators are randomly assigned to each text instance, and transcribe the text only when they can read it, skipping it otherwise to prevent guessing. We then compare the collected transcripts with the ground-truth (GT) transcript, and regard text instance as identified when they match. Stage 1 (cropped LR text). We crop each text instance from its LR patch using the annotated polygon, yielding cropped LR text image that contains no context outside the text itself. Instances identified at this stage are assigned Level 1. Since they are read from the text alone, we regard Level 1 instances as locally recoverable text. Stage 2 (full LR patch). Stage 2 begins after Stage 1 is completed for all instances. We show each remaining instance again within its full LR patch, with its text region highlighted, so that annotators can use the surrounding context. When they can read the text, annotators also select which cue helped them most: image context, when the cue comes from what else is visible in the patch, such as the same text appearing in another region; logical patterns, when it comes from regularity that the text follows, such as the numeric sequence on ruler; or prior knowledge, when it comes from what the annotator already knows, such as brand logo. Instances identified at this stage are assigned Level 2. Since they are read only once the surrounding context is available, we regard Level 2 instances as reasoning-required text. The rest are assigned Level 3. Since none of our annotators can read them even with the context, we treat Level 3 instances as unrecoverable text. For Level 3 instances, an SR output that happens to match the GT transcript cannot be distinguished from lucky guess. We therefore exclude Level 3 instances from evaluation and discard LRHR pairs containing only Level 3 instances. The resulting benchmark contains 513 LRHR pairs with 2,463 text instances (Level 1: 1,754, Level 2: 709). Further details are provided in Appendix A.1. 3.2 GTTCA Metric Existing TAISR works [15, 23] evaluate text restoration quality using text spotting models [20, 46], which jointly perform text detection and recognition on the SR output. Building on the reliable annotations of ReasonText, we propose Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), which extends the recognition-based evaluation of STISR [4, 32] to the full-image setting of TAISR. GTTCA crops each text instance with its ground-truth (GT) polygon, removing the detection stage from the measurement. GTTCA is computed in four steps (see Figure in Appendix). For each text instance, we (1) crop the SR output around its GT polygon with padding, (2) rotate and flip the crop according to its GT orientation so that the text reads upright, (3) recognize the text in the crop with an OCR model, and (4) check whether the recognized text exactly matches the GT transcript after normalization, following the standard STISR protocol [4, 32]. GTTCA is the fraction of matched instances. We report GTTCA separately on Level 1 and Level 2 instances, as well as over both levels (Overall), using PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 [6] as the OCR model. Further details are provided in Appendix A.2. 3.3 SR Models Fail on Reasoning-Required Text We evaluate twelve recent publicly available real-world SR and TAISR models on ReasonText, covering five groups: (A) GAN-based [16, 33], (B) multi-step diffusion-based [5, 9, 17, 41], (C) fewstep diffusion-based [34, 37, 43], (D) AR-based [35], and (E) TAISR1 [15, 23]. We report fidelity (PSNR and SSIM on the channel), perceptual quality (reference-based LPIPS [45] and DISTS [7], and no-reference MANIQA [39], MUSIQ [14], and CLIP-IQA [30]), and text restoration quality (GTTCA). We also report all metrics on the HR images as reference (HR oracle). Table 1 reports the results, and qualitative results are shown in Appendix A.3. Finding 1: All models struggle on reasoning-required text. GTTCA drops sharply from Level 1 to Level 2 for all twelve models, regardless of architecture, training paradigm, or whether the model is explicitly text-aware. The drop is large enough that the score ranges of the two levels do not overlap. The lowest Level 1 score (45.72%) still exceeds the highest Level 2 score (24.54%). Since the HR oracle reaches 90.69% on Level 2, far above every SR model, the gap reflects limitation of the SR models rather than of the text recognizer behind the metric. Finding 3: Better conventional SR quality does not mean better text restoration. We compute the Pearson and Spearman rank correlation between each conventional metric and overall GTTCA across the twelve models. None of them tracks text restoration quality. PSNR and SSIM show no positive correlation with GTTCA. LPIPS and DISTS, for which lower is better, correlate in the wrong direction. No-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) metrics correlate only weakly. Improving conventional SR quality therefore does not carry over to text restoration, which has to be measured on its own. Together, these findings answer the question we posed: TAISR does need reasoning. What remains is how to supply it, which we address next.

sections.title: 4 Reasoning Transfer via Captioning
sections.content: Reasoning can happen inside the SR model or outside it. The internal approach gives the SR model itself the ability to reason. The external approach obtains reasoning from an external model and injects it into the SR model. The internal approach is appealing but currently hard to pursue. Finding 3 shows that the conventional quality criteria that SR training pursues do not track text restoration, and Finding 2 shows that even text-specific modules and objectives do not help on reasoning-required text. This leaves no obvious training signal for teaching an SR model to infer locally illegible text, which motivates our external approach. This approach raises two questions. (i) Reasoning generation. What kind of reasoning-aware representation should we extract from the LR image? (ii) Injection. How should this representation be injected into the SR model so that it restores reasoning-required text? The design space for both questions is broad. reasoning-aware representation could take many forms, such as similar image retrieved from an external source, text string inferred from the LR image, or features taken from the reasoning model itself. Each of these could in turn be injected in different ways, for example by concatenating it with the SR models intermediate features, attending to it in cross-attention layer, or passing it as the models text input. Rather than exploring this space exhaustively, we derive method from two empirical observations. The first settles both design questions, and the second makes the resulting choice practical. 6 Table 3: The reasoning prompt substantially improves MLLMs on reasoning-required (Level 2) text, where OCR models and the no-reasoning prompt lag far behind. (Left) Text recall of dedicated OCR models. (Right) Text recall of MLLMs under the no-reasoning / reasoning prompts. Best per column in bold. : higher is better. Since this channel is already in place, we examine whether it can carry reasoning-aware information. To test this, we inject the GT transcripts of ReasonText directly into the caption. Given the transcripts t1, t2, . . . , tn of the Level 1 and Level 2 instances in an image, we replace the default caption with natural-language caption listing them, of the form "The image with the text t1, t2, . . ., tn.", and re-evaluate on ReasonText. Table 2 shows that GTTCA improves for every model on both levels. The gains on Level 2 are substantial. DiT4SR [9] gains over 22 points, from 24.54% to 46.71%, and SUPIR [41] and UniT [15] gain over 16 points each. As side effect, NR-IQA scores drop for several models. We attribute the drop to the caption no longer describing the scene, since these models are trained with scene-describing captions. Adding scene description largely restores NR-IQA (Appendix B.1), and the RTC caption therefore includes one alongside the inferred text (Section 4.3). This observation settles both design questions. For injection, we pass the reasoning-aware representation through the text channel that text-conditioned SR models already provide. For reasoning generation, the reasoning-aware representation is natural-language caption listing the GT transcripts of the image. In real-world scenario, however, the GT transcripts of an LR image are unavailable, so we need way to approximate this caption from the LR image alone, which we address next. 4.2 Observation 2: MLLMs Can Approximate Ground-Truth Transcripts Choosing reasoning generator. How can we obtain GT transcripts from an LR image? We measure models ability to do so with text recall, the fraction of GT transcripts that exactly match word in its output, after both are normalized. We start with OCR models [6, 8, 46], the standard tool for reading text from images, and run them on the LR images of ReasonText. Table 3 shows that their recall drops sharply on Level 2, where even the best model reaches only 44.43%. Despite the rich priors from large image-text corpora, OCR models struggle with reasoning-required text, which makes them unsuitable as reasoning generator. We therefore turn to MLLMs, which read text as OCR models do but can also reason about the image [21, 42]. We run Qwen2.5-VL [2], which UniT adopts, together with two more recent MLLMs, Qwen3.5 [29] and Gemma 4 [12]. Each model is run under two prompts. The no-reasoning prompt instructs the model to list the text it can see, and the reasoning prompt additionally instructs it to infer text using image context, logical patterns, or prior knowledge. Table 3 shows that the reasoning prompt improves every model at both levels, and the gain is larger on Level 2 than on Level 1 in all three cases. Gemma 4 reaches the highest score, 70.38% on Level 2, which exceeds the best OCR model by 25.95 points. It misses some reasoning-required text, but reads large portion of it. We therefore adopt Gemma 4 with the reasoning prompt as our reasoning generator, and use the transcripts it reads to build the caption. Does the gain come from reasoning? One might ask whether the high Level 2 recall of Gemma 4 comes from something other than reasoning, and two explanations stand out. It may be exceptional local text recognition, strong enough to read from the text region alone what our annotators could not. Or it may be memorization, since ReasonText is built on the publicly available RealSR-v3 and DRealSR, which the model could have seen during pre-training. 7 Figure 3: Gemma 4 reads locally illegible text by reasoning over relevant cues. Top: given only the target region (the locally illegible "4"), Gemma 4 fails. Adding random unrelated patches does not help, but adding the related numeric column "1""8" restores the correct reading. Bottom: likewise, "WHEY" is read only when the banner "70% BETTER THAN WHEY" is visible. Blue and red backgrounds mark correct and incorrect readings. To test the first, we mask everything outside the GT text regions, which removes the surrounding scene while leaving the text pixels intact, and run the same model on the masked images. The effect differs sharply between the two levels. Level 1 recall drops only slightly, from 86.72% to 82.55%, since locally recoverable text does not need the surroundings. In contrast, Level 2 recall collapses, from 70.38% to 29.90%. If Gemma 4 were simply strong local text recognizer, masking the surroundings would barely change Level 2 recall, just as it barely changes Level 1 recall. The collapse rules out the first explanation, since Gemma 4 clearly needs the surroundings to read reasoning-required text. To test the second, we vary the visible surrounding region (Figure 3). Gemma 4 recovers the correct transcript on Target w/ cues, where only the target text and the relevant cues are visible. In contrast, it fails on Target w/ rand. parts, where the cues are replaced by random regions of the same area, and on Target-only, the masked setting used above. This argues against the second explanation, since model recalling memorized image would not depend on the cue region in particular. With both alternatives unlikely, reasoning over the surroundings remains the most plausible explanation. 4.3 Method: Reasoning Transfer via Captioning Section 4.1 showed that caption carrying the GT transcripts improves the restoration of reasoningrequired text, and Section 4.2 showed that an MLLM with the reasoning prompt can infer most of those transcripts from the LR image. Putting the two together gives Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC). Given an LR image xLR, RTC proceeds in two steps. 1. Caption by reasoning. Query an MLLM with xLR and the reasoning prompt, which returns two sentence caption c: scene description followed by the inferred transcripts. 2. Restore by conditioning. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: 5.1 Experimental Settings We attach RTC to the six text-conditioned SR models of Section 4.1. For each model, the baseline is its official inference pipeline with its default caption source, such as LLaVA-1.5 for DiT4SR and Qwen2.5-VL for UniT. +RTC replaces only this caption with the one Gemma 4 produces under the reasoning prompt, leaving everything else unchanged. For controlled comparison, we precompute one caption per LR image and feed the same caption to all six models, keeping it fixed throughout denoising. We evaluate on ReasonText with the metrics of Section 3.3 and run all experiments on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Table 4 reports the results, and Figure 4 shows qualitative comparisons. 5.2 Results RTC recovers most of the gains observed with GT transcripts. RTC replaces the GT transcripts with transcripts inferred by an MLLM, so we first check whether the observations made with GT transcripts still hold under this replacement. Table 4 shows that they do. RTC improves GTTCA for every model on both levels, whether the model was designed for real-world SR or for TAISR. As with GT transcripts, the gains are larger on Level 2 than on Level 1 for most models, reaching 21.30 points for DiT4SR (from 24.54% to 45.84%). Moreover, the scene description in the RTC caption largely avoids the NR-IQA drop observed with transcript-only captions, and fidelity and reference-based perceptual metrics also remain stable. RTC is thus practical method that needs neither GT transcripts nor training, and it improves the restoration of reasoning-required text, where all SR models struggle, while preserving general image quality. With RTC, real-world SR model surpasses TAISR model. Without RTC, UniT achieves the best overall GTTCA, ahead of DiT4SR, which shares the same backbone but has no text-aware module. With RTC, however, the order reverses. DiT4SR + RTC outperforms UniT + RTC on both levels, even though both receive the same caption. This suggests that the current text-aware design is not complementary to reasoning, since model without it performs better once reasoning is supplied. We therefore argue for rethinking text-aware design with reasoning as its core axis. Generalization and robustness of RTC. The gains of RTC are not specific to ReasonText. On the existing TAISR benchmarks, SA-Text-test and RealText, RTC improves text restoration for all six models under their original evaluation protocol. RTC is also robust to imperfect captions. Even when Gemma 4 misreads the text with spelling errors, RTC still improves GTTCA, since the SR models can often restore the correct text. RTC therefore does not lower text restoration accuracy even when the MLLM misreads the text. Detailed results are provided in Appendix C. 9 Figure 4: Qualitative results of RTC across reasoning types. For Level 2 instances of each reasoning type, the top and bottom rows show the outputs of six text-conditioned SR models without and with RTC, respectively. With RTC, some models can turn incorrect text into correct text.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: We asked whether text-aware image super-resolution needs reasoning. To answer this, we introduced ReasonText, benchmark that separates reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text, and GTTCA, metric that measures text restoration quality without detection errors. With these tools, we found that twelve recent SR models, including those designed for text, all struggle on reasoningrequired text. As remedy, we proposed RTC, training-free plug-in, based on two observations: (i) text-conditioned SR models restore text substantially better when their captions contain the GT transcripts, and (ii) MLLMs can infer these transcripts from the LR image through reasoning. In our experiments, RTC consistently improves text restoration for both real-world SR and TAISR models, especially on reasoning-required text. Moreover, with RTC, real-world SR model surpasses TAISR model built on the same backbone, which suggests that reasoning should be core axis of text-aware design. While our study shows that TAISR needs reasoning, several limitations remain. First, ReasonText is human-curated and built on existing real-world SR benchmarks, so it is limited in size and scope. It contains 513 LRHR pairs of natural images and annotates only alphanumeric text, leaving other scripts unannotated. Future work can extend it to more languages, larger scale, more diverse domains, and revisit Level 3 with larger or more specialized annotator pool. Second, even the best model with RTC remains far below the HR oracle on Level 2 (45.84% versus 90.69%). Most of this gap therefore lies not in reading the text but in rendering it, calling for SR models that faithfully render the given text as well as better ways of bringing reasoning into SR, including internal approaches. Finally, RTC applies only to text-conditioned SR models and cannot be used with SR models that have no text channel. more general way of injecting reasoning, applicable to any SR model, is left for future work.

sections.title: A Additional Details on TAISR Needs Reasoning
sections.content: A.1 ReasonText Benchmark This section details the construction of ReasonText (Section 3.1). HR image annotation. Three annotators participate in HR image annotation, and both annotation tasks below follow the same procedure. One annotator labels all instances in pass, and second annotator reviews the pass and corrects any label they find incorrect. The two then alternate, each reviewing the others corrections, until pass ends with no change. third annotator reviews the converged labels, and any instance they flag is resolved by discussion among all three. 1. Text polygons. Annotators draw word-level polygon around every legible alphanumeric text instance in each HR image, including curved and perspective-distorted ones. Each polygon uses as many points as needed to enclose the text and nothing else. 2. Transcripts and orientations. Annotators transcribe each text instance and record the transformation that brings it upright, consisting of rotation from {0, 90, 180, 270} and an optional horizontal flip. LRHR patch construction. Existing TAISR benchmarks [23] obtain LRHR pairs by random cropping. We find that random cropping often removes the surrounding context that humans use to read locally unreadable text, turning reasoning-required instance into an unrecoverable one. We therefore crop patches manually, with three annotators participating in this stage. For each text instance in an HR image, annotators draw square crop that includes any content related to that instance, and record its coordinates. When no such content is present, the annotators draw random square crop containing the instance. Two constraints apply: the crop must be at least 512512, and it must enclose the target text polygon. Since crop is drawn for every text instance, many of the resulting crops overlap. Among overlapping crops with similar size, we automatically keep the one containing the most text instances and discard the others. We then map the coordinates of each retained crop to the 4 LR image provided by RealSR-v3 [3] and DRealSR [36] by dividing them by four, and crop the corresponding LR region. Since crop sizes vary, we finally resize the HR crop to 512 512 and the LR crop to 128 128, obtaining the standard 4 SR setting used in prior work [15, 23]. HR patch re-annotation. Cropping can cut text instance at the patch boundary, leaving polygon that extends beyond the patch or word that is only partially visible. We therefore re-annotate the instances that cross patch boundary, adjusting each polygon to the visible extent and relabeling its transcript accordingly. This re-annotation follows the same procedure as the HR image annotation, with two annotators alternating corrections until pass ends with no change, followed by review by third annotator whose flagged instances are resolved by discussion among all three. Design choices for difficulty labeling. We make three core design choices that apply to both stages of Section 3.1. (1) We assign level to an instance when any of the five annotators identifies it, rather than requiring agreement among them. (2) We select ten annotators for whom English is either native language or primary second language. Otherwise, an annotator unfamiliar with English would fail to read instances that others can read, pushing these instances to higher level and shrinking the set of instances the benchmark can evaluate. (3) We require all labeling sessions to be conducted offline without internet access. Since ReasonText is built on the publicly available RealSR-v3 [3] and DRealSR [36], searching the web with an LR patch could retrieve its HR counterpart and expose the transcript. An instance resolved this way would be recorded as readable even when no cue in the image supports it, mixing looked-up text into the reasoning-required set. Cue aggregation in Stage 2. reasoning-required instance can be read through more than one route. For example, one annotator may identify text from repeated word elsewhere in the patch, while another identifies the same text from brand they recognize. We therefore do not assign single cue to an instance. Instead, we take the union of the cues selected by the annotators who identified the instance. Each text instance is cropped around its GT polygon with padding, rotated and flipped with its GT orientation, and recognized by an OCR model. We further validate the design of GTTCA (Section 3.2) with two experiments. Ablation of the GTTCA protocol. GTTCA differs from an end-to-end text spotting protocol in two ways: it uses GT polygons instead of text detector, and it rotates and flips each crop with the GT orientation so that the text reads upright. sections.title: B Additional Details on Reasoning Transfer via Captioning
sections.content: B.1 Observation 1: Ground-Truth Transcripts Improve Text Restoration This section provides two ablations on the GT transcript caption of Section 4.1, one on its format and one on adding scene description. Caption format ablation. Text-conditioned SR models differ in the caption format they are trained with. It is therefore unclear whether the GT transcripts should be injected in each models trainingtime format or in single unified format. We compare three formats that mirror the conventions of existing SR models, namely (1) tag style GT (space), which separates the transcripts with spaces [15] ("t1 t2 tn"), (2) tag style GT (comma), which separates them with commas [37] ("t1, t2, , tn"), and (3) caption style GT, which lists them in natural-language caption ("The image with the text t1, t2, , tn."). Table shows that GT transcripts improve GTTCA over the original caption for every model, regardless of the format. Among the three formats, the natural-language caption achieves the best GTTCA for every model on both levels, even for UniT and OSEDiff, whose own conventions are tag style. We hypothesize that this is because the text-to-image models underlying these SR models were pretrained on natural-language captions, even though the SR models were later fine-tuned with various caption formats. These results support our choice in Section 4.1 to inject the GT transcripts as natural-language caption. Scene description ablation. While GT transcripts improve GTTCA, they lower NR-IQA scores for most models  (Table 2)  . We hypothesize that this drop arises because transcript-only caption departs from the captions these models are trained with, which mostly describe the scene. To test this, we prepend one-sentence scene description of each LR image, generated by Gemma 4, to the caption-style GT. Table shows that the scene description largely recovers NR-IQA. The scene description also changes GTTCA. It lowers overall GTTCA by 1.2 to 2.1 points for SUPIR, FaithDiff, OSEDiff, and TeReDiff, whereas it leaves DiT4SR nearly unchanged and improves UniT on both levels. We attribute this difference to the text encoders of the underlying text-to-image models. Table G: Adding scene description to the caption-style GT largely recovers no-reference perceptual quality. We further break down Gemma 4s Level 2 text recall by the annotated cue (288 image-context, 246 logical-pattern, and 414 prior-knowledge instances, where an instance can carry more than one cue). Recall is highest for image context (81.9%), where the cue is visible elsewhere in the image, and similar for logical patterns (69.5%) and prior knowledge (69.1%). If data contamination drove the performance, prior knowledge, the cue most tied to pre-training data, would likely be read best. Instead, it is read no better than logical patterns. Together with the analysis in Section 4.2, this suggests that Gemma 4s Level 2 recall comes from reasoning over the image rather than from memorization. B.3 Method: Reasoning Transfer via Captioning The reasoning prompt asks the MLLM for two-sentence caption. The first sentence describes the scene, which avoids most of the NR-IQA drop observed with transcript-only captions (Appendix B.1). The second sentence lists the transcripts inferred from the LR image. Figure illustrates the overall pipeline with an example caption.

In all four settings, RTC improves all six text-conditioned SR models without exception, indicating that its gains are not an artifact of particular benchmark or metric. Moreover, UniT outperforms DiT4SR in every setting without RTC, whereas DiT4SR + RTC outperforms UniT + RTC in every setting. This reproduces the reversal observed on ReasonText (Section 5.2) and again suggests that reasoning should be core axis of text-aware design. RTC is robust to imperfect captions. Since RTC feeds the SR model caption predicted by an MLLM, one might worry that wrong prediction would degrade restoration. To examine this, we split the 709 Level 2 instances by whether the RTC caption contains the correct GT transcript, into Gemma correct subset (499 instances) and Gemma wrong subset (210 instances), and measure Level 2 GTTCA on each subset before and after RTC (Table I(a)). Even on the Gemma wrong subset, RTC improves GTTCA for all six SR models. Half of the wrong captions are near-misses that differ from the GT transcript by at most two letters, and the gain concentrates on them (17.8% to 25.9%), since the SR models can still restore the exact text from near-correct caption together with the LR image (Table I(b)). For captions farther from the GT transcript, RTC still does not lower GTTCA on average (10.2% to 11.6%). RTC is therefore robust to imperfect captions, which matters in practice since the MLLM may misread degraded text. RTC remains effective on Level 3 text. ReasonTexts Level 3 comprises text that none of our annotators could read even from the full LR patch, so it is excluded from our main evaluation. Nonetheless, since RTC injects an MLLM caption that may be wrong, natural concern is that it might harm this hardest case. Table (a) shows that it does not. RTC improves GTTCA on Level 3 for all six SR models, though by less than on the other levels on average. These gains are possible because Gemma 4 with the reasoning prompt still recalls 40.2% of Level 3 text (Table J(b)). We attribute this to how Level 3 is defined. Level 3 means that none of our annotators could read the text, not that the text is intrinsically unrecoverable. This set is therefore heterogeneous. Some instances, such as serial numbers, are genuinely unrecoverable, while others might have been read by larger annotator pool or by domain experts with the relevant prior knowledge. Gemma 4 likely reads some instances of the latter kind, reflecting the limitation of our annotation protocol noted in Section 6.

sections.title: D Limitations and Broader Impact
sections.content: Limitations. We summarize the limitations discussed in Section 6. First, ReasonText is humancurated and built on existing real-world SR benchmarks, so it is limited in size and scope, with 513 LRHR pairs of natural images and only alphanumeric text annotated. Second, even the best model with RTC remains far below the HR oracle on Level 2 (45.84% versus 90.69%). Since the same model reaches at most 47.70% even with GT transcripts (Table G), most of this gap lies not in reading the text but in rendering it, and stronger MLLM alone would bring limited gains. Third, RTC applies only to text-conditioned SR models and cannot be used with SR models that have no text channel. Broader Impact. By enabling SR models to recover text that was previously unreadable from local pixels alone, this work has the potential to benefit wide range of socially valuable applications. Improved restoration of degraded text can (i) support accessibility for users with low vision by making blurred signs, labels, and documents legible, (ii) aid cultural and historical preservation by helping recover text in old photographs, archival scans, and damaged manuscripts, and (iii) contribute to public safety and navigation through clearer recovery of road signs, transit information, and emergency notices captured under poor imaging conditions. More broadly, our findings suggest that reasoning, rather than purely local perception, is productive direction for restoration tasks, encouraging the community to explore restoration pipelines that integrate world knowledge and contextual understanding. At the same time, text restored through reasoning is plausible inference rather than evidence, and it may occasionally diverge from the true content. Such outputs should not be treated as ground truth in high-stakes settings such as forensic analysis or document verification, and the ability to read degraded text calls for care with images containing private information, such as license plates or personal documents. The decoupled design of RTC helps mitigate these risks, since the MLLM caption exposes the inferred text and makes it possible to trace which component caused an error. Overall, we hope ReasonText, GTTCA, and RTC together provide constructive foundation for building TAISR systems that are not only sharper, but also more thoughtful about the text they restore.
